comparison: Both evaluate experimental design and initial clustering (C1-C4 in OpenEval; C1-C13 in peer review). OpenEval focuses on methodology and QC details, while peer review encompasses broader clustering approach including marker-based identification. Both find the approach SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers noting it 'builds on a strong foundation of literature.'

OpenEval R2 addresses initial clustering and cell type identification (C5-C13), which overlaps substantially with peer R1 (C1-C13). Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of marker usage and cluster exclusion decisions, while peer review affirms the overall clustering strategy without specific critique.

Perfect claim overlap (C14-C18) regarding neuronal cell type identification methodology. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes systematic approach and validation against published abundances, while peer reviewers affirm that 'well-established neuronal markers allow transcriptomic analyses to match clusters to specific spinal neuron subtypes.'

Perfect claim overlap (C19-C28) on v2a subtype identification and gjd2b marker discovery. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval details the validation evidence (in situ, consistency with adult fish), while peer reviewers implicitly accept findings without challenge.

Perfect claim overlap (C29-C30) on functional characterization of v2a subtypes from prior literature. OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED contextual citations, but peer review marks as UNCERTAIN with explicit disagreement: one reviewer argued 'Type I V2a neurons are more analogous to PMns than Type II' based on recruitment patterns during swimming. This represents a significant disagreement on functional interpretation.

Perfect claim overlap (C31-C36) on CoLo identification and chga marker validation. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval details multiple validation lines (transcriptomic, spatial, colocalization), while peer reviewers implicitly accept without critique.

Perfect claim overlap (C37-C42) on DoLA identification and pnoca marker. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes functional speculation is appropriately tentative, peer reviewers accept findings without challenging speculative elements.

Perfect claim overlap (C43-C54) on novel interneuron type identification with mammalian v0c homology. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of transcriptomic and morphological evidence, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'one transcriptomic cluster reveals presence in zebrafish of a spinal neuron subtype previously identified in mammals.'

Perfect claim overlap (C55-C59) on motor neuron isolation strategy. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the rigor of dual computational/experimental approach, peer reviewers accept methodology without critique.

Perfect claim overlap (C60-C71) on PMn/SMn marker distinction using chga and nr2f1a. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval details spatial validation and cell count consistency, peer reviewers affirm discovery of 'molecular distinctions causally related to unique physiology of PMn function.'

Perfect claim overlap (C72-C76) on SMn subtype markers. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes correspondence to transgenic lines and tentative speculation about muscle targets, peer reviewers accept without challenge.

Perfect claim overlap (C77-C87) on differential expression analysis and functional gene enrichment in PMns vs SMns. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval details statistical approach and functional interpretation, peer reviewers explicitly affirm discovery of 'two functional groups or cassettes of genes related to excitability and vesicle release.'

Perfect claim overlap (C88-C94) on ion channel cassette identification and validation in PMns. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. Perfect claim overlap (C95-C97) on cassette expression in escape circuit interneurons. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. Perfect claim overlap (C98-C102) on synthesis linking transcriptomic profiles to functional properties. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval connects findings to prior electrophysiology, peer reviewers affirm as central finding with one noting 'this finding will be important to the field.'
